title: The Mountain Serpent's Secret Part
markdown:
The sun was only a pink-and-gold rumor when Ivo sat bolt upright. Something electric was in the air, sharp as a new key. He sprang from the blankets, bare feet thumping the wooden floor, and went straight to his father’s workbench. Among gleaming brass and intricate springs lay a small velvet pouch: the locksmith’s most trusted tools, the ones for delicate daring work. Ivo stuffed it into his pocket. The weight sat there like a secret.

Cool morning air kissed his cheeks. Dewdrops sparkled on the grass. The town was still hushed; baking bread drifted from a nearby shop and did nothing to calm the flutter in his chest. He sped toward the tram station. Ren, the tram conductor’s niece, was already there, face a picture of urgent worry. Her bright keen eyes met his, and he knew.

“The brake part,” she blurted, a rapid whisper. “The big crucial one for the Mountain Serpent tram. Gone. Vanished before the morning run.” She wrung her hands. Her usual steady calm had cracked.

The Mountain Serpent: that grand abandoned line coiling up the jagged peaks like a sleeping dragon. Dread and excitement arrived together.

“Gone? The first run is in two hours. The whole town’s transport depends on it.”

“Exactly. Without the brake it’s a danger. A runaway waiting to happen.”

Ivo’s mind raced faster than any tram. “The old workshop. At the top of the abandoned line. That’s where they kept spares. Your uncle always talked about it.”

Ren’s eyes widened. “That line hasn’t run in years. Rickety. Broken. Tracks twisted. The wind up there is wicked.”

“Precisely.” He grinned, determined. “We’ll take the other tram. The sturdy one in the lower yard. Ride it up. Find the part. Bring it back. Quick and quiet.”

She glanced at the daunting peaks, then at his unwavering face. Her jaw set. “All right. If we don’t act, it’s a disaster. Let’s get that part.”

They clambered into the silent dusty tram in the lower yard. Seats worn smooth from countless ordinary journeys now held a secret one. Ivo, with nimble fingers and a spark of his father’s genius, coaxed the controls to life. A lurch, a groan, then motion, slow at first, then gathering speed. They were on the abandoned line. Tracks creaked and protested, a symphony of metal on rust. Wind whipped through open windows, tugging hair, whispering mountain secrets. Birds chirped morning songs, oblivious to the high-stakes journey above.

Below, the town began to stir, tiny lights blinking awake like sleepy fireflies. They climbed into the heart of the awakening day. Peaks pierced a rosy sky now painted with vibrant orange and deep purple. Wind howled, a mighty beast trying to push them back. Ivo kept the tram steady, knuckles white on the controls. Ren, with her keen eye for detail, pointed out loose bolts and swayed sections of track, her knowledge invaluable. They were a team, determined, battling the elements without making a speech about it.

Then a sharp jolt. The tram shuddered to a halt. A vital connection had snapped. Metal shrieked. Wind seemed to laugh. Panic flickered in Ren’s eyes. A knot tightened in Ivo’s stomach. He gripped his father’s tools, cool metal a familiar comfort.

“Hold on.” He leaped out, heart pounding, scrambled under the tram. Gravel scraped his hands. The special wrench, heavy and particular, was in his palm. Sparks flew. Metal groaned. A moment stretched taut.

A click. A solid, satisfying clunk. The connection held. Ivo scrambled back inside, breathless and exhilarated. “We’re moving again.”

They jolted forward, faster now, the summit within sight. The old workshop perched precariously on the mountainside like a determined bird’s nest. They crashed to a halt just outside, the tram groaning in relief. Inside, dusty shelves lined the walls, piled high with forgotten parts. Cobwebs draped everything like ghostly curtains. Ivo and Ren searched with frantic energy, eyes darting from shelf to shelf.

Ren gasped, pointing. There it was: the massive gleaming brake part, exactly what they needed, sitting as if it had been waiting just for them. Triumph surged, quiet and practical. The sun had fully risen, painting the entire world in brilliant dazzling hues. They had made it with time enough, if the descent held.

They wrapped it in old canvas and clambered back in. Descent was swift and sure. The mountain’s grip loosened. The town spread bright and welcoming below. They glided into the station, wheels singing, just as the first morning commuters gathered, yawning, none the wiser.

Ivo and Ren exchanged a look: a shared secret, etched in sunlight on metal and the thrum of a tram that would, in an hour, carry the town as if nothing had happened. Ivo touched the velvet pouch in his pocket. The tools had done the work they were made for. The morning, already loud with bread and birds, could keep its ordinary face.
characters: Ivo (the locksmith's son), Ren (the tram conductor's niece)
